passage:
Sunday: At the family lunch, Bua announces that cousin Mohit got 96 in maths. Papa turns to Amandeep. 'And you? 81? See, Mohit studies.' Amandeep smiles, pushes rice around the plate, and leaves half.
Wednesday: After school, Amandeep sits at the desk doing extra sums nobody set, lips pressed tight. When Mummy peeks in, Amandeep says, 'I'll beat Mohit next time,' but slams the book when one sum goes wrong.
Saturday: Mohit phones to ask for help with a drawing project. Amandeep helps, then asks Mummy quietly, 'Would you love me more if I was Mohit?' Mummy sits down and takes Amandeep's hand. 'Never. Marks are not you.'

qa.q: What did Mohit score in maths?
qa.a: Mohit got 96 in maths.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Papa compared the marks at lunch?
qa.a: Amandeep felt hurt and embarrassed, hiding it behind a smile and leaving half the rice.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently when marks come up at family lunches?
qa.a: Talk about Amandeep's own effort and progress in private, instead of holding up Mohit as the standard in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Mohit be affected by always being held up as the example?
qa.a: Mohit might feel awkward or pressured to keep scoring high, and the comparisons could make things tense between the cousins.

grounding: Shows a child whose score is compared with a cousin's and who reacts with both extra effort and a quiet hurt about not being enough.

passage: Suraj, you think your Nani never had a bad report card? Sit. When I was nine, in our big house in Jabalpur, my cousin Kamla came first every year. Every evening Tauji would say, 'Look at Kamla, Minakshi, and look at you.' So I started waking at five to study, and yes, my sums got better. But I also stopped singing, because Kamla sang better too. One day Masi found me crying behind the water tank. No lecture. Masi only asked, 'Kamla is Kamla. What do you like?' I said, 'Drawing.' The next week Masi bought me a tin of colours. I still have that tin.

qa.q: What did Masi buy for young Minakshi?
qa.a: Masi bought a tin of colours.

qa.q: How did young Minakshi feel about being compared to Kamla every evening?
qa.a: She felt hurt and never good enough; she pushed herself to study at five in the morning, but stopped singing and ended up crying behind the water tank.

qa.q: Which turning point in the story helped young Minakshi most, and why?
qa.a: Masi asking what she liked instead of lecturing, because it gave her something of her own that was not a contest with Kamla.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt hearing Tauji hold up the marks every evening?
qa.a: Kamla may have felt proud but also uneasy, and the constant comparison could have put distance between the two cousins.

grounding: Illustrates a child compared with a higher-scoring cousin who feels both driven to work harder and a quiet hurt of never being enough.

passage:
At Sunday lunch in Teta's flat in Marseille, Aunt Samira passed the couscous and said, "Rosa got the highest maths mark in her class again. Twenty out of twenty!"

Everyone clapped. Nour's cousin Rosa went pink.

Nour, ten, looked at her plate. Her own test, fourteen out of twenty, was folded in her school bag. On Friday she had been proud of it.

"And Nour?" someone asked.

"Fourteen," she said quietly.

"Good, good," said Teta, and reached for the bread.

On the bus home Nour unfolded the test and studied the two questions she'd got wrong. Part of her wanted to beat Rosa next time. Part of her just wanted Friday's feeling back.

qa.q: What mark did Nour get on her test?
qa.a: Nour got fourteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Nour have on the bus home?
qa.a: Nour felt hurt that her proud Friday feeling had faded, and also motivated, wanting to beat Rosa next time.

qa.q: What small step would help Nour hold on to her pride?
qa.a: Keep her own progress in view, like the fourteen she was proud of on Friday, and fix the two wrong questions for herself rather than only to beat Rosa.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel when everyone claps?
qa.a: Rosa went pink, so she may feel pleased and embarrassed at once, and perhaps awkward next to Nour.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a cousin praised for a higher score and feeling both hurt and a push to do better.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting in Class 5B, Mummy perched on a small chair and listened to Miss Fernandes.

"Madhuri is bright, but she talks a lot during reading time."

Mummy sighed. "Her cousin Francis is in 5A, and his teacher says he never speaks out of turn. Why can't you be like Francis, Madhuri?"

Madhuri studied the chart of planets on the wall. Her ears were hot.

Miss Fernandes said gently, "Madhuri also helps the new girl every day at lunch."

Mummy blinked. "Oh. She never told me."

In the corridor, Madhuri decided two things: she would try to be quieter in reading time, and she would never mention Francis at home again.

qa.q: Which class is Francis in?
qa.a: Francis is in 5A.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as she studied the chart of planets?
qa.a: Madhuri felt embarrassed and hurt at being compared to Francis in front of her teacher; her ears were hot.

qa.q: How could Mummy support Madhuri instead of comparing?
qa.a: Talk about Madhuri's own behaviour and strengths, like helping the new girl, without holding Francis up as the measure.

qa.q: What would change if Miss Fernandes hadn't mentioned the lunchtime helping?
qa.a: Madhuri might have left believing she is simply worse than Francis, with nothing good in her noticed.

grounding: Shows a child compared to a better-behaved cousin, with the comparison stirring both effort and a quiet hurt.

passage:
Diwali: "Your cousin Pooja came first in her school quiz," Bua announced over the sweets. Ishita, eleven, clapped with everyone, then went and sat by the diyas alone.

Two weeks later: Ishita stayed up with her general-knowledge book every night, whispering capitals to herself. Mummy found her asleep on it.

A month later: Ishita came second in her own school quiz. She ran home waving the certificate. Dadi smiled and said, "Very good! Pooja came first, na?"

Ishita slid the certificate into her drawer, under her socks, and didn't take it out again.

qa.q: Where did Ishita put her certificate?
qa.a: Ishita slid the certificate into her drawer, under her socks.

qa.q: Why did Ishita hide the certificate after Dadi's reply?
qa.a: Ishita felt deflated and not good enough; even her best result was measured against Pooja, so the pride drained away.

qa.q: What could Dadi have said instead?
qa.a: Simply celebrate Ishita's second place and ask how she prepared, leaving Pooja out of it.

qa.q: What would change if the family praised each child's own effort?
qa.a: Ishita's late-night drive could stay joyful instead of turning into a quiet feeling that she will never be enough.

grounding: Shows constant comparison with a cousin first driving a child to work harder and then leaving a quiet sense of never being enough.

passage: Avni, you're crying because your mother said your cousin got better marks? Come, sit near your Dolma Ama. When I was a girl of ten, in our big house in Kalimpong, there were nine of us cousins. My cousin Pema was the clever one. Every night at dinner, my uncle said, "Pema came first. What about you, Dolma?" I would push my momos around the plate. Some days it made me study harder, I won't lie. I stayed up with a candle. But mostly I felt I was never enough, whatever I did. One day I came second in the district drawing contest. My uncle asked if Pema had entered. I tore up the certificate. Then Pema found the pieces, stuck them together and put it on her wall. "You draw better than me," she said. I never forgot that.

qa.q: What did Dolma come second in?
qa.a: The district drawing contest.

qa.q: How did young Dolma feel at dinner when her uncle compared her with Pema?
qa.a: She felt hurt and not good enough, pushing her momos around, even if it sometimes made her study harder.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dolma Ama's story?
qa.a: Pema sticking the torn certificate together and saying Dolma drew better, which showed Dolma her own worth apart from the comparison.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt being the one everyone praised?
qa.a: Pema might have felt uncomfortable being used to measure Dolma, and caring enough to show she admired Dolma's drawing.

grounding: It illustrates a child compared to a cousin who feels both motivated and hurt, and a quiet sense of never being enough.
